items.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
items.summary:
With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing?

The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time.

Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

items.title: Alibris has made a deal to sell used books on Temu.
items.summary:
As Sam Spratford reports in Publisher’s Weekly , Alibris has inked a deal to make over a million books available on Temu’s massive digital marketplace. It’s not too shocking, as Alibris seems to be chasing a model of breadth and speed; the company partnered with fast fashion brand Shein last year.

Temu already sell books, though they’re mostly craft and hobby titles, many coming from overseas. The deal with Alibris is part of Temu’s Local Seller program, meaning the listings won’t affect the supply chain: books will be sourced, stored, and shipped locally in the US.

Temu (originally a play on “Team Up, Price Down”) has become a shorthand for crappy quality and weird knock-offs. It’s also been dogged by accusations of breaching data privacy and intellectual property, not to mention other bad practices; among other things, a congressional study found a high risk of forced labor in their supply line.

We’ll have to see how it works out, but it seems like expansion to a larger online footprint through consolidation or partnership is the preferred business plan for digital retailers these days. With Goliaths like Amazon out there, I get the logic, but it’s always a little dispiriting to see everything, including used books, getting funneled into the same few buckets.
items.t: Alibris has made a deal to sell used books on Temu.

items.title: Put off Bolaño’s 2666 for too long? In 2027, tackle it with the Equator book club.
items.summary:
The Equator reading group is back by popular demand.

After a successful summer outing with Mike Davis’s Late Victorian Holocausts , the globally minded magazine is sponsoring another book club. This time, the subject is a literary doorstop—Roberto Bolaño’s 2666 .

Why read 2666 in a flock? Bolaño’s final novel, published posthumously, is famous for exasperating as often as it rewards. Appropriately, this reading group has a questing name: “ Into the Abyss .”

As Sam Anderson noted in a review for New York , in 2666 the late Chilean maestro “follows his restless talent down every available rabbit hole of improvisation, no matter how dark and unpromising.” Over the novel’s near thousand pages, “single sentences stretch on…obsessively sifting the most minor gradations.”

The sum total is “indisputably brilliant,” but also “crowded, brutal, dense.”

A novel like this rewards accountability mechanisms, and deserves plenty of conversation. (That’s the bet Equator has made, anyway.) Readers who’ve been ISO buddies to sift through all the brilliance can now sign up for five discussion sessions that break the book up into 150 page chunks.

Periodic club meetings will be moderated by scholars, fans, and special guests. And I do mean special. Rachel Kushner, Karl Ove Knausgård, Benjamin Kunkel, Pankaj Mishra, and Bolaño translator Natasha Wimmer anchor a starry slate of speakers.

But perhaps most exciting is the discussion framework. Over its five sessions, “Into the Abyss” will consider the novel through its many thematic lenses.

items.title: 7 Books About Mothers with Voracious Interior Lives
items.summary:
The political project constraining American women, the one that gave us Dobbs , rests on a picture of motherhood as a woman’s entirety. Instinctive, total, self-abnegating, and therefore requiring no compensation, no consent, and no interior life. A reader of feminist theory may hear Silvia Federici’s “Wages Against Housework”: Housework “transformed into a natural attribute of our female physique and personality” so that it could go unpaid. “They say it is love. We say it is unwaged work.” Fifty years ago, Adrienne Rich named it the institution of motherhood—distinct from the experience—and the institution now has a legislative program foisted on us by predators. 

Every book on this list documents a mother who is also something else. Voracious. Desiring. Fixated on a dead poet, a diary, a theology, a body’s capacity for harm. Sometimes in psychosis. Sometimes distracted by thoughts which have nothing to do with the baby. The obsession is evidence of an interior life beyond motherhood, whatever its perils. 

I know this fixation from the inside. Sleepless with an infant, I became obsessed with an ancient mother goddess named Cybele, and I followed her from Galicia to the archives of the Louvre while examining my own Cuban matrilineage. The memoir that came of it is Desire Lines . 

Whether memoir, or essay, or confession, or autotheory, or hybrid of essay and autofiction, every one of these books is a mother’s account of a life that did not stop with the arrival of her child. They are literature first. Their political force follows from their craft. Propaganda simplifies…

items.title: The Most Read Books on Goodreads This Week
items.summary:
There’s no question what the most read book of the moment is: the title that took the #1 spot this time has almost triple the readers of the book in the #2 spot. We do have one change-up in the top five since last week. Can you guess the 2025 novel that’s risen in popularity recently? Here’s a hint: the movie adaptation comes out later this month.

Two New Books Out This Week You Should Know About 

Unfortunately, the most read books on Goodreads tend not to be diverse by any definition of the word. So, here are a couple of new books out this week that deserve wider readership.

Take My Word for It: A Memoir by LeVar Burton, Tracey Michae’l Lewis-Giggetts 
 Very few actors have been front and center in so many culturally historic moments as LeVar Burton. From playing Kunta Kinte on Roots to Geordi La Forge on Star Trek , and being the host on Reading Rainbow —one might even say that Burton has embodied and portrayed many aspects of America’s past, present, and its (hopeful) future. Here, he traces his life, first as a child experiencing the Civil Rights Movement, then his acting career, and later his advocacy for literacy. He fills in the moments in between his major roles to show the struggle and resilience it has taken to lead such a remarkable life. —Erica Ezeifedi

Bones of Jade, Flesh Like Ice by Gracie Marsden 
 You don’t often come across historical fantasy inspired by Taiwanese mythology and the enthusiasm around this debut novel is big. Yu’er’s story unfolds in the Eleventh century in a small village. First sold off for marriage in her youth at the advice of a…

items.title: The Most Beautifully Illustrated Manga
items.summary:
If you’re an art lover, you probably frequent museums and galleries. Likely, you also have a penchant for browsing through biographies about the masters. Mayhaps you’re even a fan of picture books, coffee table books, or any sort of book where art plays a large role. But do you know what art form you may be missing? Manga.

Most of this Japanese genre conforms to a very specific art style developed in the late nineteenth century, so even if you’re not a reader, you can spot manga when you see it. According to Denise Tempone , it consists of expressive eyes, slender silhouettes, and cartoonish characters in realistic settings, among other traits. Combined, these characteristics have made manga an extremely recognizable genre worldwide — and for good reason. Before I even knew what manga was, I, a child in Argentina, could always pinpoint what I then called “ Sailor Moon -like art”.

Still, not all manga are created equal. The four titles I gathered here are all distinctive: they take these traits and make them theirs. From astounding brushwork to coziness incarnate, these manga will make you want to hang them on your walls just to stare at them in wonder.

If you do decide to give manga a try (assuming you haven’t already, and I’ve been preaching to the choir this whole time!), then not only will you be treated to some truly stunning art, but you’ll also get a thrilling story to go with it. That’s a win-win if I ever saw one.

items.title: 3 Indigenous Horror Audiobooks
items.summary:
Across Turtle Island, Indigenous horror is doing something truly spectacular. These writers aren’t just telling great stories; they’re using their talents to do something truly unique. They combine both supernatural and very real lived realities to tell stories that highlight Indigenous experiences across the continent. These authors often tackle major themes like ancestral and inherited grief and resilience in the face of the horrors of ongoing colonial violence. These stories are well-crafted gems, terrifying in the best possible way. Combine them with a talented narrator, and you have a thrilling audiobook perfect for autumn listening. Here are a few to get you started.

Bad Cree by Jessica Johns, Narrated by Tanis Parenteau 
 Tanis Parenteau brilliantly performs this debut novel that is one part horror and one part family story. It begins one morning when Mackenzie wakes up from a nightmare with a dead crow’s head in her hands. She decides to go home and consult with the elders in her community to try to figure out why these dreams keep haunting her. This decision sets off a series of events that will force Mackenzie to confront the grief she’s been carrying for far too long. Parenteau’s performance captures the tension created by Mackenzie’s anxiety and fear of the supernatural occurrences around her. Her voice allows the horror to creep up on the listener. I was terrified in the best way possible.

items.title: What is the Best Literary TV Adaptation of All Time? Day Five
items.summary:
Well, well, well, if it isn’t the semifinals, the thing I mix up with the quarterfinals every time we do one of these brackets. We’re down to four shows, in two match-ups—and these are not the four shows I expected. Who knows where this will go.

A lot of heartbreak yesterday, with four great shows dropping out:

– Orange in the New Black was denied parole;

– Shogun failed to unite the warring states;

– Slow Horses got demoted to an even more degrading and menial desk job, under an even grosser and meaner boss;

– And Brideshead Revisited converted back to Protestantism.

The four left standing are in two surprising match-ups. Carnage winner Roots is up against Cerebral winner Sherlock . These are two wildly different shows, though both have  launched their share of discourse over the years. Roots attracted the ire of a ton of insecure right-wing bozos, and the fights over which Sherlock guys to ship overheated a lot of Tumblr servers. Which discourse magnet do you prefer?

And Cozy winner M*A*S*H is up against Carnal winner Killing Eve . Two shows about finding connection in the trenches. The question is if Lit Hub’s readers prefer a wise-cracking friend or a wise-cracking crush?

We’re curious to see how this shakes out. Let’s vote!

–James Folta

items.title: Maia Kobabe On Advocacy, Comics Censorship, and More: Book Censorship News, November 13, 2026
items.summary:
It’s likely when you think of book bans in the 2020s, one of the books that immediately comes to mind is Gender Queer . Maia Kobabe’s memoir was published in the spring of 2019, and it not only earned tremendous critical praise, but it also landed among the 10 books honored each year as an Alex Award winner. The Alex Awards honor the best books published for adult readers with teen appeal. It’s not “just” an award. It’s a designation that helps library workers discover new titles to share with readers, both adult and young adult.

Gender Queer has since gone on to earn even more honors. In one example, the book landed on Illinois’s Lincoln List, a statewide list that encourages high schoolers to read and discuss great literature. The titles on that list are selected by librarians and educators, with space for teen readers to nominate and vote for titles they want to see on the list. Kobabe’s memoir was selected as a Teen Choice Nominee for the 2023 list.

Kobabe’s memoir explores eir gender and sexuality coming-of-age. It’s a story that teen readers of any gender or sexual orientation will connect with, as it’s also about growing up and feeling the pressures of conforming to beliefs one has learned at home and/or adapting to one’s personal experiences outside the home. Censors tend to home in on seven particular panels in the 240-page book, pointing to them as “pornographic,” as “child pornography,” as “grooming,” or any other term du jour, failing to bother talking about the other hundreds of panels, including the especially potent final scenes where Kobabe wrestles with…

items.title: Everybody’s First Drafts Are Bad
items.summary:
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s  Craft of Writing  newsletter— sign up here . 

Your first novel is the crappy scarf you make with acrylic yarn that doesn’t come out straight or even. It looks more like a river on a map than a bridge. That’s ok; you’re still proud of it and you even wear it once or twice. Eventually, it finds its way into a drawer.

You make another scarf and this one comes out better but mostly because you learned to rip out the rows that were wrong or wonky and redo them, even though that sucks and you hate it and you mourn all the wasted time it represents.

Your next couple scarves improve on that first one. Maybe you try a shawl or a more complicated stitch. You finally realize how much the quality of yarn matters and you invest in nicer stuff. But when you get home to cast on, you find that nicer yarn is the wrong weight for the project you want to do.

You’ve learned so much knitting those scarves, so you set your sights on a sweater. It’s the most advanced pattern you’ve ever tried, but not completely out of your league. You take your measurements so it has a chance of actually fitting when you finish. You love the yarn, but as you’re making progress you worry the color looked better in the shop than made up into a whole sweater. Or people don’t ohh and ahh like you thought they would when you show them your progress.

You finish the sweater. You take a selfie and put it on Instagram and it’s your most popular post ever. Everyone thinks it’s lovely! It looks so good! You could be a professional and sell them on Etsy! People would pay so much money…
items.t: Everybody’s First Drafts Are Bad

items.title: There’s Always Next Year: What the Buffalo Bills Taught Me About Writing and Hope
items.summary:
There is nothing writers love more than talking about how hard it is to write. Stephen King described the writing process as “like crossing the Atlantic Ocean in a bathtub.” Sportswriter Red Smith, in a quote often erroneously attributed to Ernest Hemingway, compared it to sitting down at a typewriter and bleeding. Gwendolyn Brooks: “Delicious agony.” George Orwell: “Like a long bout of some painful illness.”

That is also what it feels like to watch the Buffalo Bills.

Like most Bills fans, I was born into this serfdom with no possibility of escape. There is a picture of my dad, wearing a Bills sweatshirt and hat, holding two-day-old me in the hospital; just out of frame is the Bills-branded cooler of Miller Lite he brought with him to watch the Bills play the Dolphins on the hospital’s television. It was Western New York in the very late eighties. The Bills had Jim Kelly, Thurman Thomas, and Bruce Smith and were about to embark on a run that would culminate in four consecutive Super Bowl appearances; it was a bringing-beer-to-the-hospital era.

But here is where being a Bills fan works to my advantage: who cares about humiliation!

But the hospital beers couldn’t last. Those four consecutive Super Bowl appearances became four consecutive Super Bowl losses, a feat that had never happened before in the history of the NFL and has never been equaled since. The Bills are among history’s most prolific losers, the Wagners of the devastating loss; they are losing virtuosos, and they’re loud about it. Their seventeen-season-long playoff drought was one of the NFL’s longest ever,…
items.t: There’s Always Next Year: What the Buffalo Bills Taught Me About Writing and Hope

items.title: What We Lose When We Don’t Archive Black Motherhood
items.summary:
For as long as I can remember, words have been how I shaped my world. But last year I went looking and for the first time could find no words to hold or comfort me.

I was pregnant and needed a book to guide me into motherhood, one of the biggest transformations of my life. So I did what I always did as a  writer and archival filmmaker. I scoured digital and physical bookshelves for something, anything, to give me what I needed. I didn’t need reference material for my creative life but for the one I was creating. I desperately needed stories, not advice or how-tos—real, earned lived experiences and visuals. The search came up empty. There were no intimate portraits of pregnant and newly postpartum Black bodies or the vulnerable reflections of this time. A literary absence that felt intentional. How could this be? Black women had been birthing, rearing, and mothering for centuries yet documentation of our collective and individual experience couldn’t be found. I was infuriated. I ached. I had hoped that the lives of my foremothers could be a map for the one I was creating.

Like all good books,  Sasha Bonét’s The Waterbearers  found me exactly when it was supposed to. A literary balm that soothed me during the most tender time. Bonét traces and seamlessly weaves together the matriarchal stories of her own family with those of America’s matriarchs; Black women like Iberia Hampton, Camille Billups and Betty Davis. From the first page Bonét let me know that she was writing for women like me, those who were searching for something but never found what they were looking for.…
items.t: What We Lose When We Don’t Archive Black Motherhood

items.title: Can You Write a Poetry Collection That’s a Page-Turner?
items.summary:
When I began writing my second poetry collection, Future Tense , a memoir in verse, I wanted it to be the one thing I rarely hear collections called: a page-turner.

The book documents the three years I fought to become a mom while losing my own, ending with my daughter’s adoption shortly before my mom’s death. Because life was changing minute by minute, diagnosis by diagnosis, I knew the book could unfold that way too.

I wanted to build a collection that pulled readers forward—not because they needed to know what happened next, but because they needed to know what the next poem would reveal. Each poem would deepen the tangled story, creating the emotional momentum of a novel. I wanted to make readers look up to realize they’d just devoured fifty pages of poetry.

Because poetry can do this. It can move fast and deep, ask us to feel before we understand, and hold contradiction, mystery, and hard truths at once. And yet poetry has a reputation for being difficult—a slog you have to wade through rather than something you can’t wait to keep reading.

With Future Tense , I wanted to take my lifelong mission of expanding what poetry can do one step further: to show that genre doesn’t define momentum.

Here are five craft approaches, along with the questions I asked myself, for creating a poetry collection that reads with urgency and momentum.

What Makes a Story Worth Following? 

Story sticks—it’s the emotional architecture through which we view the world: what the speaker wants, what stands in her way, and what’s at stake. Plot is the specific sequence of events that forces…

items.title: How a Vanity Fair Insider Managed Hollywood Egos
items.summary:
On my first day at Vanity Fair, I received a tap on my left shoulder from a woman with cropped blond hair, a voluminous mink, and enormous black sunglasses. She looked out of sorts. “Can you tell me where my office is?” she asked. It was Tina Brown. True, the maze of indistinguishable cubicles was confusing, but was it not odd that the editor in chief didn’t know the way from the elevator to her office? I offered to guide her. I figured we would find it eventually—after all, the maze was roughly circular, designed like a dementia ward, so one eventually finds one’s room. I located her office, and she disappeared into it without a backward glance.

I asked a colleague about the incident, and she said, “Oh yes. Hap­pens all the time. Tina never knows where she is.” Sure enough, it wasn’t the last time I got “the tap.” I learned that her driver had to be given separate instructions on their destination, as she would invariably have forgotten by the time she got in the car. If she was given a note with the information, she would immediately lose it. I figured her mind was on other, more interesting, things. She had rescued the dramatically tanking reboot of Vanity Fair from imminent death and put it in the black, with a bold redesign that mixed Hollywood glitz and gossip with lengthy, in-depth articles on so-called real issues. She hired fabulous writers and photographers, causing an uproar in the magazine world by paying them unprecedented rates.

My new boss, Jane Sarkin, was wiry and intense, with a habit of chewing her hair when nervous, which was all the time. Her job was…

items.title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review – jailed in Putin’s Russia
items.summary:
The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal

Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.

The opening section of his book about the experience is gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. When he found his way into journalism in his early 20s – first working nights as an editorial assistant at the New York Times, then getting started properly as a reporter at the Moscow Times – he gravitated to Russia and fell in love with it.

items.title: Classic Mexican Books
items.summary:
My idea to compile this list of classic Mexican books first came up while I was talking about Japanese authors. I had been thinking of doing an informal miniseries where I focus on the specific literary traditions and histories of different ethnicities and nationalities, when, during a workshop I was attending, I had mentioned that the first recorded novel in history came from a Japanese noblewoman. This, of course, set us down a path of not only the history of Japanese literature, but also the context in which said novel— The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu, in case you didn’t know—sprang from. But more on that another time.

Through this conversation, I was reminded of how many people don’t know about rich literary traditions, even when—as is the case with Mexico and the U.S.—they come from nearby places. The thing with books and literature is that they are just as much of their time as they can point towards the future. Through Mexican literature, you can hear the rhythm of the pre-Columbian Nahuatl poets, feel the consequences of war and colonialism, and see what happens as a land and a people are forced to forget their language and learn a new one. And, how that new language is bent and woven through ancestral stories to make something wholly new, such as the magical realism genre, as is the case with Latin America.

You’ll see exactly what I mean in the sampling of classic Mexican books below.

Like Water for Chocolate by Laura Esquivel

items.title: Transcription by Ben Lerner audiobook review – a meditation on memory for the smartphone era
items.summary:
Actor Seth Numrich vividly captures the neurotic tendencies of a middle-aged man with a digital dependency, in an intense multilayered tale of family and storytelling

We meet the unnamed narrator of Transcription on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. He is going to interview his one-time mentor Thomas, a celebrated German writer and film-maker, who is 90 and who, owing to his age, probably won’t be interviewed again. The narrator confesses to his young daughter, Eva, that he is nervous about the meeting. Those nerves are replaced by panic when he gets to his hotel and drops his iPhone into a sink of water, rendering it useless. Not only does he have no means of recording the interview, he won’t be able to FaceTime Eva at bedtime.

Ben Lerner’s novella is a thoughtful meditation on memory, storytelling and lives lived through technology. The middle-aged narrator’s anxiety over his phone falls away as he engages with the world around him and with his past. He is pleased at being “able to convert the sense of being screenless into a kind of super­sensitivity” though later, in Thomas’s house, he finds himself “glitching, craving my cellular phone on a cellular level, shamefully unresponsive to the old media that surrounded me”. For the interview, he pretends to record the conversation on his dead phone and tries to commit Thomas’s words to memory.

Continue reading...

items.title: Broken People Don’t Break the System. Broken Systems Break the People
items.summary:
“America, The Never Event,” an excerpt from The Fleeing Season by Jamie D Brooks 

“We needed to move quickly because of the severe pelvic fracture and damage to the left kidney. It was the bleed, we had to stop the bleed. . . . Somehow, the repair to the kidney didn’t, wasn’t somehow, we . . . I . . . it was the wrong side—the wrong kidney we were trying to work on.”

I am no doctor, but I could tell that the physician’s voice was stripped raw, the way voices sandpapered by anguish often are. I understood that his 20-plus years practicing as an orthopedic trauma surgeon could weather his soul, but I detected much more than the strain of accumulated sorrow in Dr Gordon’s voice coming through my phone. Before I could ask my follow-up questions—there were so many—the fresh river of pain coursing through him gave way, breaching the composure he’d fortified through decades of delivering devastatingly bad news to the hopeful. His tears brought me right to his pain. If I wasn’t careful, I could have been swept along with him in his surging current of hurt. For the empathetic, other people’s pain can be a contagion. I resisted my reflexive urge to comfort with, “It’s okay.” It wasn’t. Dr Gordon had just described a wrong-side surgery: a medical Never Event.

In theory, as the wording suggests, Never Events should never happen. In reality, they do—a lot, or at least a lot more than we’d like to think they do. Hospitals are miraculous institutions of healing, aided by the hands of dedicated practitioners. They also can be profoundly dangerous places, their risks obscured in part by…
items.t: Broken People Don’t Break the System. Broken Systems Break the People

items.title: Exclusive Double Cover Reveal of Two Forthcoming Forrest Gander Titles
items.summary:
Electric Literature is pleased to reveal the covers of The Weight of a Frozen Moment and Dune Lines: New and Selected Poems by Forrest Gander, which will be published respectively on April 6, 2027 by Milkweed and April 27, 2027 by New Directions. You can pre-order your copies here and here . 

The Weight of a Frozen Moment 

From Pulitzer Prize-winning author Forrest Gander comes a poignant exploration of intimate human and ecological bonds. In a small intentional community in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains, two sisters—Maya and Mira—grow up sharing explorations, secrets, and the sense that their lives are unfolding in parallel. But as adolescence pulls Mira away, first subtly and then irrevocably, Maya must remake herself alone: through grief and family tragedy, through a journey to Karnataka to honor the anniversary of their father’s death, and through an ever-deepening bond with the place that helped shape her. 

Strikingly lyrical and quietly devastating, Forrest Gander’s poetic restraint and his detailed attention to the natural world imbues the landscape with a gravitational pull on the narrative. The Sierra Nevada is witness, anchor, and the ground on which the sisters find their way back to each other and to an even more expansive sense of belonging.

A meditation on place, identity, and the strength of the ties that endure, The Weight of a Frozen Moment offers unexpected grace in demonstrating what it means to be separate and inseparable.

items.title: Public Access Afterworld by Jane Schoenbrun review – horror in the TV static
items.summary:
The Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma writer-director’s first novel is a wry, hugely fun journey into the dark world behind our screens

Public Access Afterworld is the first novel by Jane Schoenbrun, director of cult-hit horror film I Saw the TV Glow and the more recent Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma; movies in which screens are a permeable barrier and people are menaced by the uncanny realms that lurk behind them. Here the main character is Bethany Peters, a young trans woman working as a content moderator at a YouTube-like company called GlobalVill. Her job is to watch “offensive, illegal, disturbing videos that have no place on the internet” and press a red button to remove those that violate the code of conduct. One night she sees a video posted by someone with the username JulesPublicAccessAfterworld, a visibly malnourished non-binary kid who reminds Bethany of herself “before her stay in hospital, and everything that happened to her there”. The kid says to camera, “If you’re watching this, David Sawyer, this is for you,” then takes out a razor blade and draws it down their arm. Soon Bethany is off on a quest to save them, in the course of which she will learn that she herself is one of “the crooked”, people destined to vanish into Public Access Afterworld, the world behind the TV screen.

There are several other strands to the novel. A nameless patient at the Saint Thomas Youth Rehabilitation Center tells us about a fellow inmate “going by the name David Sawyer” who spends every night narrating a TV programme about a character called…

items.title: Does M John Harrison’s Booker win mean science fiction is finally accepted by a ‘snobby’ literary establishment?
items.summary:
Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars

As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book.

His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse. Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Does M John Harrison’s Booker win mean science fiction is finally accepted by a ‘snobby’ literary establishment?

items.title: The Universe Needs a Software Update
items.summary:
In a Hollow at the Metaverse 

Click to enlarge 

Special Relativity 

Like others in search, I chased
rainbows, twinkles, fantasies.
Not brambles, not cathedrals,

nor hummingbirds. No time for
the bark of a sea lion,
the fragrance of fresh lemon.

I revisited Plato’s Allegory
of the Cave. Tried to improve
upon War and Peace .

Your good tentacle is waving
goodbye, Grandpa.
Forgive me—I was busy

filming a Venus flytrap
in time lapse. I lied when
I said I had no time.

items.title: ‘We are dream-walking into a desperate situation’: the Booker prize winner on his sci-fi alien invasion wakeup call
items.summary:
He is a sci-fi titan but M John Harrison has just exploded into the mainstream – with The End of Everything, an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast. Does he really think we have no hope left?

With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over.

The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize. My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. It is a bit like having coffee with a cheerier, more neatly bearded Gandalf – it will surprise no one that, in his youth, Harrison read The Lord of the Rings every year for a decade.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘We are dream-walking into a desperate situation’: the Booker prize winner on his sci-fi alien invasion wakeup call

items.title: A Beginner’s Guide to Reading and Writing Visual-Literary Hybrids
items.summary:
Adding photographs to fiction and poetry became a trend in 1990 with the explosive popularity of WG Sebald’s Vertigo , but it was far from a new innovation. There were illustrated novels 98 years earlier, starting with Georges Rodenbach’s symbolist novel Bruges-la-Morte in 1892. The writer and curator Terry Pitts keeps a list of poetry and fiction with photographs, called Vertigo, which has almost 900 titles. Today, many contemporary writers experiment with images, from Jonathan Safran Foer to Minae Mizumura, Hannah Weiner, Monica Ong, Lydia Davis, Debra Di Blasi, Susan Howe, Jesse Ball, and Ali Smith. Yet there is no book on the subject, no history, no guide. It often happens that authors who add photos to their books are inspired by just one or two precedents, so the 900 and counting exemplars represent an amazing diversity of practices. Consider Ben Lerner’s tentative, small black and white details in 10:04 alongside Teju Cole’s full-page, coated-stock professional color photos. 

I’ve been engaging with and teaching fiction with images for a decade now, and I feel like an explorer: wherever I look, there are ways of using images that I’ve never seen before. My writing students often find images liberating: suddenly their words have wordless companions. The images jostle for space on the page (where to put the photo? on a facing page? does an image in a novel get a caption?) and they speak to the reader in a completely different language, sometimes at odds with what the writer intends to communicate. I love all this, because it makes me think even more intently about…
items.t: A Beginner’s Guide to Reading and Writing Visual-Literary Hybrids

items.title: WHAT REMAINS Asks What Survives After Everything Is Lost
items.summary:
Brais Lamela’s debut novel, What Remains , opens with a lecture on forensic architecture that the novel’s narrator, a Galician PhD student living in New York, is only half listening to as he helps himself to a second serving at the lunch buffet. His attention often drifts between concerns about his dissertation, life in the city, and his increasingly serious relationship with his girlfriend, Mariana. Only later, waiting at a bus stop, does he return to the lecture and wonder: “Is it really possible to restore what’s been lost, to reconstruct places that no longer exist for the displaced, and in the process achieve some sort of justice, or at least alleviate their grief?”

The question might just as easily be asked of the narrator’s own research, which concerns a little-known episode of Spanish history: the displacement of rural communities in Galicia under Franco’s dictatorship, when villages were submerged to create hydroelectric reservoirs and their inhabitants relocated to newly constructed settlements. The novel really takes off when the narrator becomes preoccupied with a woman he discovers in the archives. Displaced from her village and resettled, she was subsequently expelled from her new home. The records document her displacement but reveal little of her life. Perhaps this is why the narrator turns to writing fiction: What begins as his attempt to write a dissertation gradually takes the shape of a novel, presumably the novel we are reading. Fiction, Lamela suggests, might offer a form of restitution in its ability to imagine what the historical record cannot…
items.t: WHAT REMAINS Asks What Survives After Everything Is Lost

items.title: Killing the Pope review – the truth behind the attempted murder of John Paul II
items.summary:
Was the failed assassination of the Polish pope a Soviet plot or simply the work of a deranged hitman?

On the afternoon of Wednesday 13 May 1981, St Peter’s Square in Rome was packed with more than 10,000 pilgrims, excited to see the charismatic John Paul II, formerly Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Kraków. Two and a half years earlier he had become the youngest cardinal to be elected pope in more than a century and the first non-Italian for 455 years.

At 5.17pm a man pulled out a concealed pistol and raised it with both hands above the heads of the crowd. He took aim at the pope, only a few metres away, and fired several shots. Then, as he backed away from the shocked bystanders, he tripped and fell, where he lay pinned to the ground by a Franciscan nun until handcuffed by uniformed police. Meanwhile the pope had been hit by two bullets, one in the arm and the other in the abdomen. He was losing blood rapidly. He was rushed to hospital and underwent an operation, before beginning a slow recovery. The would-be assassin was soon revealed to be Mehmet Ali Ağca, a member of the rightwing Turkish paramilitary group known as the Grey Wolves.

items.title: Dad Died and Everyone Is Buying Me Shots
items.summary:
An excerpt from No Such Thing as Monday by Siân Hughes 

I walked into the back room at Dad’s house about midday with his dinner on a plate covered in cling film in one hand and a bowl of crumble and custard in the other, and he was dead in his chair. His dog Lester was still tied to the leg of the chair, pulling at his lead and snarling and growling at me. I had a bag of clean laundry over one arm and the front door key balanced in the same hand as the crumble, so I sort of dithered about in the doorway, half in and half out of the hall, not knowing what to put down where or which direction to move in, forward or backward.

For some reason I felt a bit wrong turning my back on him, so I reversed a few steps into the hallway like he was royalty or something, then put the plate and bowl down on the chair by the door where he sat to take off his shoes and put on his slippers. I hung the laundry on one of the coat hooks and went back in. I swear that dog has no short-term memory. When I went back in the room it was like he’d never seen me before, and in his fury he pulled right out of his collar, across the room in one shot, diving straight at the back of my left ankle and digging his rotten old stumps of teeth into the heel of my trainer.

I approached the chair with the damn dog still attached to my heel. Maybe Dad wasn’t dead after all. Maybe he was only napping. Maybe if I held on to his hand to feel for a pulse he would wake up and take the piss out of me. He’d say, “Silly cow thought I’d kicked the bucket!” I rubbed my hands on the back of my jeans to warm them up…
items.t: Dad Died and Everyone Is Buying Me Shots
